title: Charity is friendship (ST II-II.23.1)
hookLine: Thomas calls charity friendship with God

cards: "I will not now call you servants." Jesus says it at the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, the night before he dies. "But I have called you friends."
A servant does what he's told without being let in on the plan. A friend gets told things. Thomas Aquinas takes that one word, friends, very seriously.
Back on day three hundred thirteen, charity, the love that never falls away, was the greatest of the three. When Thomas comes to it, his first question isn't whether it's a feeling, or a duty.
He asks whether charity is friendship. His answer is today's title.

teach.b: Thomas borrows Aristotle's account of friendship, in three parts. First, not every love is friendship. People love wine, Thomas says, but nobody is friends with wine.
You want it for yourself; you don't wish it well. Friendship means wanting good for the other, for their sake.

teach.h: GOOD WILL, BOTH WAYS, SOMETHING SHARED.
teach.b: Second, that good will goes both ways. A one-sided love isn't yet a friendship. Third, friends share something: a life, a work, a table.
Now Thomas lays this over God. Does God wish us well, for our sake? Yes.
Is the love returned? It can be. And what's shared?

God shares his own happiness with us. Thomas points to Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is faithful: by whom you are called unto the fellowship of his Son." So charity, for Thomas, is friendship between a person and God.
Here's what makes it bold. Aristotle doubted friendship could stretch across a gap as wide as the one between people and gods.
And Thomas raises a sharp objection against himself: friends live together, and we don't live with God. His answer: we do, already, in part. Paul again: "But our conversation is in heaven."
In that old English, conversation means the way you live, where you belong.

One more turn. Because a friend loves what belongs to the friend, charity reaches everyone God loves, even enemies, the way you'd care for a friend's children, for the friend's sake. Charity is not a mood.
It's a friendship with a wide circle.

how: Catholics speak of charity as the greatest of the theological virtues, and the Catechism, following Thomas, describes it as the virtue by which people love God above all things and their neighbor for the love of God, and, with St. Teresa of Avila, describes prayer as a close sharing between friends.

o: a two-way friendship between people and God
a servant's duty of obedience to God
being kind to friends before strangers

games.q: charity as friendship — tap the pairs.
p: wanting good for the other's sake

s: for Thomas, charity is just a warm feeling
he asks first whether charity is friendship, and answers yes: good will, returned, built on something shared.
Thomas borrows his idea of friendship from Aristotle
the three marks come from Aristotle. Thomas applies them to God.
charity, for Thomas, leaves out enemies
a friend loves what belongs to the friend, so charity reaches everyone God loves.

games.q: an objector tells Thomas that friends live together, and we don't live with God, so charity can't be friendship. what does Thomas answer?
o: we already live with God in part, and fully later.
say friendship doesn't need any shared life.
games.why: Thomas quotes Paul, "our conversation is in heaven": the shared life is begun now and finished later.

practice: Friends don't make speeches; they say what happened, what's bothering them, what made them laugh. If you pray, talk with God like that, plainly, about today, and then be quiet for a bit, the way you would with a friend.
If you don't, bring to mind one real friendship and notice its three parts: wishing them well, being wished well back, and the thing you share.

wordCard.voice: Charity is friendship. For Thomas, charity is not only kindness. It's a friendship between a person and God, built on the happiness God shares. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: charity, the love Thomas calls friendship with God.

carryVoice: Your line: friendship with God. A friend, unlike a servant, gets told things. See you tomorrow.
